title: connection churn and tcp slow-start: inference tail latency investigation
content:
Purpose
This doc captures an experiment-driven investigation into how connection churn and TCP slow-start contribute to tail latency for short inference responses (1-20 tokens). The motivation: many customer workloads are low-token, low-compute inference calls where network and transport setup dominate p95/p99 latency. We need concrete numbers and mitigation guidance for the platform and SDKs.

Background & hypothesis
- Observation: spikes in p99 for short responses often coincide with bursts of new client connections (e.g., serverless frontends, cold-started clients, aggressive connection TTLs at load balancers).
- Hypotheses:
  1) TCP slow-start and cong. control cause measurable per-request latency inflation for short-lived connections even with small payloads.
  2) TLS handshake (especially full 1-RTT) adds significant overhead when session resumption is not used.
  3) Proxies/sidecars (Envoy) and middleboxes amplify the effect because they break connection reuse or introduce extra handshakes.

Experimental setup
- Serving binary: inferd v2.3.1 (internal test build with pprof hooks enabled).
- Model: small decoder-only model that returns 5 tokens on average; mean compute time ~12ms. Kept constant to isolate network effects.
- Hardware: 8x NVIDIA A10g instances behind an NLB, serving container on GCP-like VMs (4 vCPU, 16GB RAM).
- Edge: tests run through three topologies: direct-to-service (no proxy), via Envoy sidecar (local to pod), via external ALB + Envoy (two hop).
- TLS: TLS1.3 enabled. Tests toggled between session-resumption enabled/disabled by clearing session tickets.
- Client driver: custom Go harness that can open ephemeral connections at a configured concurrency and connection rate; also can reuse connections. Repeated runs with wrk2 and ghz to sanity-check numbers.
- Kernel/TCP settings: default RTO/rate control; subsequent runs tried BBR vs Cubic; tcp_tw_reuse off.
- Metrics: per-request timings (client-side), server-reported request start/end, and tcpdump traces for round trips and initial cwnd.

Key experiments & results
1) Baseline: persistent HTTP/2 connections with multiplexing, long keepalive (idle 300s)
- median: 18ms (12ms compute + 6ms network overhead)
- p95: 34ms
- p99: 52ms
Notes: multiplexed streams amortize connection setup; p99 dominated by queueing not transport setup.

2) New TCP connection per request (simulated connection churn; keepalive disabled) with TLS session resumption allowed
- median: 38ms
- p95: 120ms
- p99: 210ms
Breakdown from tcpdump: initial SYN+SYN-ACK+TLS handshake push first packet then short application exchange. Measured TLS handshake added ~65-90ms on median for our cloud region; TCP slow-start impacted bytes-in-flight ramp for server push which added ~10-30ms depending on initial cwnd and routing.

3) New TCP connection per request + no session resumption (cold TLS)
- median: 95ms
- p95: 240ms
- p99: 390ms
TLS full handshake (1-RTT + cert verification) accounted for the bulk (120–250ms tail in our runs).

4) Envoy sidecar in path, connection churn at client (single-use TCP connections to Envoy; Envoy multiplexes to upstream)
- median: 45ms
- p95: 150ms
- p99: 280ms
Finding: if client churns connections to Envoy, Envoy's upstream pools still hid some of the upstream TLS cost, but added thread/context switching and additional packet processing. When Envoy had to establish upstream TLS connections (under load spikes) we observed head-of-line effects that amplified p99.

5) QUIC (HTTP/3) experiments against a QUIC-enabled edge (0-RTT session resumption enabled)
- median: 25ms
- p95: 48ms
- p99: 85ms
QUIC significantly reduced handshake tails due to 0-RTT resume and better connection migration handling. However, early data replay concerns required conservative application-layer idempotency checks, so not always usable for all clients.

TCP initial cwnd sensitivity
- We ran small microbenchmarks varying initial cwnd from 2 MSS to 10 MSS. For 5-token responses the extra RTTs due to low initial cwnd added up to 8–30ms depending on payload size and path RTT. BBR vs Cubic had modest effects on tail for short flows.

Other observations
- RST/FIN churn: aggressive client-side short-lived connections cause socket churn and increased CPU on Envoy (ephemeral socket handling), correlating with higher queuing delays and p99 spikes.
- TLS session ticket size and frequency: frequent key rotation on the server (for security/compliance) reduced resumption effectiveness and increased cold-handshake incidence.
- Middleboxes: certain corporate proxies strip TLS session tickets or reject 0-RTT, increasing cold-handshake percentage for some enterprise customers.

Recommendations (practical mitigations)
1) SDK/Client-side
  - Default to HTTP/2 with connection pooling and long keepalives for SDKs used in short-inference paths. Make pooling the default for JS/Python/Go SDKs.
  - Expose helper to pre-warm a small connection pool on app startup (2-4 connections). For serverless, add an optional warmup call during cold-start.
  - Implement retry semantics that are 0-RTT aware (avoid unsafe retries when using early data).
2) Platform/Edge
  - Enable TLS1.3 session tickets and reasonable session ticket lifetime; coordinate ticket rotation with support SRE to avoid too-frequent rotation.
  - Prefer QUIC-enabled edge for regions with high connection churn customers; roll out in beta to customers who can tolerate early-data considerations.
  - Tune Envoy upstream pool sizes and connection timeouts to avoid upstream churn during traffic spikes; monitor Envoy socket churn metrics and CPU.
3) Infra & kernel
  - Tune initial cwnd to 10 MSS on inference nodes (needs validation per network provider).
  - Consider enabling TCP Fast Open where supported (requires client support).

Tradeoffs & caveats
- Longer keepalives/pooling increases resource surface (file descriptors, idle connections), which interacts with Dedicated/reserved capacity. Need quota/capacity planning.
- QUIC reduces handshake tail but introduces implementation complexity and telemetry gaps (different stack). Client compatibility is a known blocker for some customers behind restrictive proxies.
- Increasing initial cwnd can slightly increase congestion risk for larger flows, but for our short response use-case it seems net positive. Validate per-provider.

Open questions / next steps
- Measure effect across more cloud regions and real customer network paths (some enterprise proxies break resumption).
- Automated e2e test in staging that simulates high churn for serverless frontends to watch p99 and Envoy CPU.
- Cost model: quantify the incremental compute/FD cost for keeping pools open at scale vs p99 latency savings. This should feed into SDK defaults and platform quotas.
- Explore an opt-in "connection-warmup" facility on the Redwood Console for new Dedicated clusters where we pre-establish a fleet of warmed upstream connections on customer bootstrap.

Appendix: quick commands and notes
- tcpdump one-liner used: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap \"host <client> and host <server>\"
- Go harness repo: github.com/redwood-inference/conn-bench (branch: churn-experiments)
- Envoy config knobs observed to help: upstream_http2_max_concurrent_streams, connection_idle_timeout, connection_reuse_policy tweaks.

Notes to reviewers
- This is a working doc. Numbers are from ~30 runs per topology; variance is non-trivial across regions. Prioritize validation on customer-similar networks before wide rollout.
- If we agree on the recommendations I can open follow-up tasks: SDK change, Envoy tuning PR, console warmup prototype.

Unresolved items for follow-up:
- Should we default Node SDK to HTTP/2 pooling or be conservative and keep TLS session resumption only? (Priya to owner decision)
- How aggressive can we be with initial cwnd across our cloud providers without causing regressions for larger/streaming workloads?
